content:
My draft on the smooth/compact induction functor will be available very soon, but I have struggled quite a while in giving them suitable names. Here are several choices:

  1. In literature we use Ind for the smooth induction and c-Ind for the compact induction, so we may use SmRep.Ind for the smooth induction and SmRep.cInd for the compact induction.
  2. the smooth induction is constructed by taking smooth vectors fromcoind so we give it SmRep.smCoind; the compact induction is constructed from ind when the morphism between topological groups is an open map, so it sould be SmRep.openInd. Once the scalar map is an open map, Rep.ind automatically sends smooth representations to smooth representations and we can deduce the adjunction easily, so the name compact is probably mathmatically misleading. For the case we use the compact induction in reality, we actually mean the induction from the compact OPEN subgroups.
  3. use SmRep.coind SmRep.ind.

Which should be the best one?
In what generality do the definitions (a) work and (b) make mathematical sense?

s : H ->* G a morphism of topological groups.

  1. For the restriction functor: s is continuous for (a) (b)

  2. For the smooth induction fuctor: no restriction on s for (a); for (b) you need continuity of s to get the adjunction

  3. For the "compact" induction functor: s is an open map for (a); for (b) you need "s is open and continuous" to get the adjunction. In particular, H may NOT be a subgroup or compact. The finiteness is absorbed in the definition of MonoidAlgebra k[G] which we use to construct the algebraic induced representation.
